statement:
A rooted tree has n nodes, numbered 0 .. n-1, given by a parent array parent: parent[v] is the parent of node v, and the root's parent is -1. The numbering comes with no ordering guarantee; a parent may have a larger id than its child. The depth of node v is the number of edges on the way from v to the root; the root has depth 0. The node reached by walking k edges up from v along parent pointers is called the k-th ancestor of v; in this problem, k = 0 means v itself, i.e. a node is its own ancestor.

Size: 1 <= n <= 2 * 10**5, and at most 2 * 10**5 queries in total. The tree can be very deep: a chain of 2 * 10**5 nodes is a valid input. So "walk up the parent pointers one step at a time for each query" is not good enough: on a chain a single query takes O(n) steps, and all the queries together take 4×1010 steps. Requirement: O(nlogn) construction and O(logn) per query.

Part 1 — The k-th ancestor

class RootedTree:
    def __init__(self, parent: list[int]) -> None: ...
    def kth_ancestor(self, v: int, k: int) -> int: ...   # the node k edges above v, or -1 if there is none

The constructor must check that parent really describes a rooted tree and raise ValueError otherwise. It is valid when: exactly one position holds -1 (that is the root); every other position holds a node id in [0, n); and every node eventually reaches the root by following parent pointers. An empty list, two roots, a node that is its own parent, and several nodes whose parent pointers form a cycle are all invalid.

kth_ancestor(v, k): for k = 0, return v; when k is at most the depth of v, return the corresponding ancestor; when k is greater than the depth of v, return -1. k can be very large (say 10**18). Raise IndexError if v is not in [0, n); raise ValueError if k < 0.

All three parts use the same tree as the example:

parent = [3, 0, 0, -1, 3, 4, 4, 6, 1]          # n = 9, the root is node 3

                3                depth 0
              /   \
             0     4             depth 1
            / \   / \
           1   2 5   6           depth 2
           |         |
           8         7           depth 3

kth_ancestor(8, 0) == 8
kth_ancestor(8, 1) == 1
kth_ancestor(8, 2) == 0
kth_ancestor(8, 3) == 3
kth_ancestor(8, 4) == -1        # node 8 has depth 3, so it has no 4th ancestor
kth_ancestor(5, 2) == 3
kth_ancestor(3, 0) == 3
kth_ancestor(3, 1) == -1        # the root has no parent

Part 2 — Lowest common ancestor and distance

    def lca(self, u: int, v: int) -> int: ...        # lowest common ancestor of u and v
    def distance(self, u: int, v: int) -> int: ...   # number of edges on the path between u and v

The lowest common ancestor (LCA) of u and v is the deepest node that is an ancestor of both. Since a node is its own ancestor, lca(u, u) == u; if u itself is an ancestor of v, then lca(u, v) == u. Between two nodes of a tree there is exactly one path that does not repeat a node: go up from u to the LCA, then down to v. distance(u, v) is the number of edges on this path, and distance(u, u) == 0. Raise IndexError for ids outside [0, n). Both functions must be O(logn) per call.

lca(8, 2) == 0        distance(8, 2) == 3        # path 8 - 1 - 0 - 2
lca(8, 7) == 3        distance(8, 7) == 6        # path 8 - 1 - 0 - 3 - 4 - 6 - 7
lca(5, 7) == 4        distance(5, 7) == 3        # path 5 - 4 - 6 - 7
lca(6, 7) == 6        distance(6, 7) == 1        # 6 itself is an ancestor of 7
lca(3, 8) == 3        distance(3, 8) == 3        # 3 is the root
lca(7, 7) == 7        distance(7, 7) == 0

Part 3 — The maximum edge weight on a path

    def __init__(self, parent: list[int], weight: list[int] | None = None) -> None: ...
    def path_max(self, u: int, v: int) -> int | None: ...

Now every edge has an integer weight: weight[v] is the weight of the edge between v and parent[v], in [-10**9, 10**9]; weights may be negative and may repeat. weight[root] belongs to no edge and its value is ignored. If the length of weight is not n, the constructor raises ValueError.

path_max(u, v) returns the largest edge weight on the path from u to v. When u == v the path has no edges; return None. Raise IndexError for ids outside [0, n); calling path_max when no weight was given at construction raises ValueError. Each call must again be O(logn), with no more than O(nlogn) extra preprocessing.

path_max(2, 7) == 5          # 1, 4, 2, 3, 5

path_max(6, 7) == 5          # only one edge
path_max(7, 7) is None       # no edges
solution:
Before writing any code, clarify four things. Is the numbering ordered? (No: a parent's id can be larger, so you can't assume that "processing nodes in increasing id order means the parent was already processed".) How deep can the tree be? (It can be a chain, so depths can't be computed recursively, and queries can't walk one step at a time.) Does a node count as its own ancestor? (Yes; this determines the answers for lca(u, u) and for the case where "u is an ancestor of v".) Is the input guaranteed to be valid? (No; the constructor has to check.)

All three parts use the same idea: binary lifting. Precompute, for every node, "where do I land after jumping up 1,2,4,8,… edges"; any upward jump of any length can then be broken into at most log2​n such jumps.

Part 1

Compute depths first, checking the input along the way. Build each node's list of children from parent, then run a breadth-first search (BFS) from the root, using a list as the queue. No recursion: Python's default recursion limit is 1000 frames, so a chain of 2 * 10**5 nodes would raise RecursionError right away (the verification code demonstrates this). After the BFS, if the number of visited nodes is not n, some node can't reach the root. At that point every non-root node has a valid parent, so walking up from a node that never reaches the root never stops, which means it must be going around a cycle; this one check therefore covers both "a node is its own parent" and "several nodes form a cycle".

The lifting table. up[j][v] is the node reached by jumping 2j edges up from v; if the root is reached before the jump is complete, it stops at the root. So that "stop at the root" needs no special-casing, the table records the root's parent as the root itself. Then we have the recurrence

up[j][v]=up[j−1][up[j−1][v]],

i.e. jumping 2j edges is the same as jumping 2j−1 edges twice in a row. It holds near the root too: if the first jump already stops at the root, the second jump starts from the root and still stops at the root.

How many levels: the maximum depth is n−1, so take the smallest LOG >= 1 with 2LOG>n−1, i.e. max(1, (n - 1).bit_length()). For n=2×105, LOG = 18.

Queries. First compare k with depth[v]: if k is larger, return -1 immediately. Otherwise k <= depth[v] <= n - 1 < 2**LOG; write k in binary and, for every bit j that is 1, jump 2j once. The jumps add up to exactly k, and the order in which the bits are taken doesn't matter. Comparing with the depth first does two things: an input like k = 10**18 never touches a level that doesn't exist; and the "stopped at the root" values in the table are never mistakenly returned as answers.

Cost: building the table takes LOG list comprehensions of length n, so O(nlogn) time and memory; a query takes at most LOG jumps, O(logn).

class RootedTree:
    """A rooted tree given by its parent array. up[j][v] is the node 2**j edges above v, clamped at the
    root: inside the table the root is its own parent, so a jump that would leave the tree stays put."""

    def __init__(self, parent: list[int]) -> None:
        n = len(parent)
        roots = [v for v in range(n) if parent[v] == -1]
        if len(roots) != 1:
            raise ValueError(f"expected exactly one root, found {len(roots)}")
        root = roots[0]
        children: list[list[int]] = [[] for _ in range(n)]
        for v, p in enumerate(parent):
            if v == root:
                continue
            if not 0 <= p < n:
                raise ValueError(f"parent[{v}] = {p} is not a node")
            children[p].append(v)
        depth = [0] * n
        order = [root]                    # BFS order; the list is its own queue
        for u in order:                   # NOTE: no recursion -- a path of 2 * 10**5 nodes is a legal input
            for c in children[u]:
                depth[c] = depth[u] + 1
                order.append(c)
        if len(order) != n:               # an unreached node can only be walking around a cycle
            raise ValueError("some node does not reach the root")
        self.n, self.root, self.depth, self.order = n, root, depth, order
        self.log = max(1, (n - 1).bit_length())      # smallest LOG >= 1 with 2**LOG > n - 1 >= every depth
        first = list(parent)
        first[root] = root                # NOTE: the root points at itself, so every jump clamps for free
        self.up = [first]
        for _ in range(1, self.log):
            prev = self.up[-1]
            self.up.append([prev[a] for a in prev])  # 2**j edges = 2**(j-1) edges, twice

    def _check_node(self, v: int) -> None:
        if not 0 <= v < self.n:
            raise IndexError(f"node {v} out of range [0, {self.n})")

    def kth_ancestor(self, v: int, k: int) -> int:
        self._check_node(v)
        if k < 0:
            raise ValueError("k must be non-negative")
        if k > self.depth[v]:
            return -1                     # NOTE: decided by depth alone, which also guarantees k < 2**LOG
        j = 0
        while k:
            if k & 1:
                v = self.up[j][v]
            k >>= 1
            j += 1
        return v

Part 2

Two steps.

Step 1: bring both to the same depth. Jump the deeper node up by depth[u] - depth[v] edges, which is just one Part 1 query. If the two nodes now coincide, the originally shallower one is an ancestor of the other, and it is the answer.

Step 2: jump both nodes up together. Now u != v and they have the same depth. Say each still has to walk up t edges to reach the LCA, with t≥1 but unknown. The key property is monotonicity: after walking up s edges together, the two nodes are different when s<t and the same when s≥t (once two paths merge they never separate again, and the stopped-at-the-root values in the table satisfy this too). We want to walk exactly t−1 edges and stop right below the LCA. The method is to try bit by bit from the highest to the lowest: if after jumping 2j together the two nodes are still different, jump; otherwise don't.

Invariant: before processing bit j, let r be "how many more edges until right below the LCA"; then 0≤r<2j+1. Initially r=t−1≤depth−1<2LOG, so it holds. "Still different after jumping 2j" is equivalent to 2j<r+1, i.e. 2j≤r: in that case we jump, and after subtracting 2j, r is less than 2j; otherwise r was already less than 2j. Either way the invariant holds for j−1. After processing bit 0, r<1, i.e. r=0: the two nodes sit exactly on two different children of the LCA, and the answer is up[0][u].

If you instead "binary search on s, calling kth_ancestor each time", the result is also correct, but each query is O(log2n); trying bit by bit scans the levels only once, O(logn).

The distance follows directly from depths: u is depth[u] - depth[a] edges from the LCA, and v is depth[v] - depth[a] edges from it.

def lca(self, u: int, v: int) -> int:
    self._check_node(u)
    self._check_node(v)
    depth, up = self.depth, self.up
    if depth[u] < depth[v]:
        u, v = v, u
    u = self.kth_ancestor(u, depth[u] - depth[v])    # both are now at the same depth
    if u == v:
        return u                                     # one of them was an ancestor of the other
    for j in range(self.log - 1, -1, -1):
        if up[j][u] != up[j][v]:                     # NOTE: jump only while the two stay different,
            u, v = up[j][u], up[j][v]                #       so the loop ends one edge below the answer
    return up[0][u]


def distance(self, u: int, v: int) -> int:
    a = self.lca(u, v)
    return self.depth[u] + self.depth[v] - 2 * self.depth[a]


RootedTree.lca = lca
RootedTree.distance = distance

Part 3

The path u → v consists of two "upward" walks: u to the LCA and v to the LCA. Both lengths can be computed from depths, so the problem becomes: walking k edges up from x, what is the largest weight among those edges?

This is the same decomposition as Part 1, except that each jump also needs to know the maximum over the edges it covers. Build a second table: mx[j][v] is the largest weight among the 2j edges going up from v, with the recurrence

mx[j][v]=max(mx[j−1][v], mx[j−1][up[j−1][v]]),

taking the maximum of the first 2j−1 edges and of the second 2j−1 edges. The root's slot is filled with −∞: there are no edges above the root, so when the root is reached before 2j edges, the remaining part only picks up −∞, which doesn't affect the maximum. At query time, split k into binary and update the answer with the corresponding mx[j][v] on every jump; these blocks don't overlap and together make up exactly those k edges.

When u == v both walks have length 0 and there are no edges, so per the statement return None; in every other case the path has at least one edge, so the result is always some edge's weight, never −∞. One path_max is one lca plus two upward walks, O(logn); the extra memory is a second n×LOG table.

NEG_INF = float("-inf")


class RootedTree(RootedTree):
    """Adds edge weights. mx[j][v] is the largest weight among the 2**j edges going up from v (fewer if
    the root comes first: the root's own slot holds -inf, which never wins a max)."""

    def __init__(self, parent: list[int], weight: list[int] | None = None) -> None:
        super().__init__(parent)
        self.mx = None
        if weight is None:
            return
        if len(weight) != self.n:
            raise ValueError("weight must have one entry per node")
        first = list(weight)
        first[self.root] = NEG_INF        # NOTE: weight[root] belongs to no edge
        self.mx = [first]
        for j in range(1, self.log):
            below, half = self.mx[-1], self.up[j - 1]
            self.mx.append([max(m, below[a]) for m, a in zip(below, half)])

    def _max_up(self, v: int, k: int):
        """Largest weight among the k edges going up from v (-inf when k == 0). Needs k <= depth[v]."""
        best = NEG_INF
        j = 0
        while k:
            if k & 1:
                best = max(best, self.mx[j][v])   # NOTE: read the block's maximum BEFORE leaving v
                v = self.up[j][v]
            k >>= 1
            j += 1
        return best

    def path_max(self, u: int, v: int) -> int | None:
        if self.mx is None:
            raise ValueError("the tree was built without weights")
        a = self.lca(u, v)                # also validates u and v
        if u == v:
            return None                   # the path has no edge
        return max(self._max_up(u, self.depth[u] - self.depth[a]),
                   self._max_up(v, self.depth[v] - self.depth[a]))

Follow-ups

  • When don't you need the table? When the tree is shallow. Walking up the parent pointers one step at a time costs O(h) per query, where h is the height of the tree. If the tree is balanced (h=O(logn)), the naive approach has the same query cost as binary lifting, needs only O(n) memory, and the code is much shorter. It also isn't worth building the table when there are few queries: building it takes nlogn operations, while all queries together only walk q⋅h steps. Binary lifting pays off only when "the tree may be deep and there are many queries", so in the interview you should ask for these two numbers first.
  • How much memory does the table use, and can you save some? The table has n×LOG entries: 3.6×106 for n=2×105. In CPython each entry is an 8-byte pointer, so the rows of the up table alone add up to about 29 MB, and with weights mx takes as much again. As NumPy int32 arrays it is 14.4 MB, and the build can be vectorized to one line, up[j] = up[j-1][up[j-1]]. Saving more means changing the structure: store for each node only one pointer "B=⌈n​⌉ edges up"; at query time take big jumps first, then walk the remaining fewer-than-B edges one step at a time. Memory drops to O(n) and a query becomes O(n​): for n=2×105, B=448, at most about 900 steps, versus 18 for binary lifting. That is a direct trade between memory and query time.
  • What if the aggregate is a sum instead of a maximum? You don't need a second table. Compute pre[v] (the sum of edge weights from v to the root) in BFS order; the path sum from u to v is then pre[u] + pre[v] - 2 * pre[lca(u, v)], with O(n) extra memory. This works because addition has an inverse, so you can subtract the part above the LCA that was counted twice; maximum has no inverse, and "the maximum from the root to u" can't tell you which part lies above the LCA, which is why you need the table stored in blocks.
  • What if the tree changes? It depends on the change. Adding a leaf is cheap: the new node's entry at each level depends only on its ancestors, whose entries already exist, so you add one entry per level. Only when the node count grows past 2LOG do you have to build one more level for all nodes, which happens once each time the node count doubles, so amortised each leaf addition is O(logn). Changing an edge's weight doesn't work this way: every entry in mx that covers this edge has to change, in the worst case the whole subtree times the number of levels. For sums, you can flatten the tree into an array by DFS entry/exit times and use a Fenwick tree for "add to a whole subtree, query a single point"; for maxima you need heavy-light decomposition plus a segment tree, and queries become O(log2n). Re-parenting a node requires a dedicated dynamic-tree structure such as a link-cut tree.
  • If you only need the LCA, are there other approaches? Two common ones. One writes the tree's Euler tour as an array, turning LCA into a range minimum on the array, which a sparse table handles with O(nlogn) preprocessing and O(1) queries; its queries are faster than binary lifting, but it can't answer "k-th ancestor" or "path maximum". The other, when all queries are known in advance, is Tarjan's offline algorithm: one DFS plus union-find, with nearly linear total cost. The strength of binary lifting is that a single table supports all three kinds of queries, and online.

The code below corresponds to the "sum" and "adding a leaf" follow-ups; the verification code checks both.

def root_prefix_sums(tree: RootedTree, weight: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    """pre[v] = total weight of the edges from v up to the root (0 for the root itself)."""
    pre = [0] * tree.n
    for v in tree.order[1:]:              # BFS order: a parent is always filled in before its children
        pre[v] = pre[tree.up[0][v]] + weight[v]
    return pre


def path_sum(tree: RootedTree, pre: list[int], u: int, v: int) -> int:
    return pre[u] + pre[v] - 2 * pre[tree.lca(u, v)]


class GrowingTree(RootedTree):
    """Adds add_leaf(): a new node's rows depend only on its ancestors' rows, which already exist."""

    def add_leaf(self, p: int, w: int = 0) -> int:
        self._check_node(p)
        v = self.n
        if self.n >= 1 << self.log:                   # keep 2**LOG > n - 1: one more level, for everyone
            top = self.up[-1]
            if self.mx is not None:
                self.mx.append([max(m, self.mx[-1][a]) for m, a in zip(self.mx[-1], top)])
            self.up.append([top[a] for a in top])
            self.log += 1
        self.n += 1
        self.depth.append(self.depth[p] + 1)
        self.order.append(v)                          # appending keeps "parents before children"
        self.up[0].append(p)
        for j in range(1, self.log):
            self.up[j].append(self.up[j - 1][self.up[j - 1][v]])
        if self.mx is not None:
            self.mx[0].append(w)
            for j in range(1, self.log):
                self.mx[j].append(max(self.mx[j - 1][v], self.mx[j - 1][self.up[j - 1][v]]))
        return v

# --- an independent brute force: nothing but single parent-pointer steps ---
def _chain(parent, v):
    """v, its parent, ..., the root."""
    out = [v]
    while parent[out[-1]] != -1:
        out.append(parent[out[-1]])
    return out


def _brute_kth(parent, v, k):
    chain = _chain(parent, v)
    return chain[k] if k < len(chain) else -1


def _brute_lca(parent, u, v):
    above_u = set(_chain(parent, u))
    return next(a for a in _chain(parent, v) if a in above_u)


def _brute_path_weights(parent, weight, u, v):
    a = _brute_lca(parent, u, v)
    out = []
    for x in (u, v):
        while x != a:
            out.append(weight[x])
            x = parent[x]
    return out


def _random_tree(rng, n, shape):
    """A parent array of the given shape with shuffled labels (so a parent's id is not smaller than its
    child's). `par` is written over positions 0..n-1, position 0 being the root."""
    if shape == "random":
        par = [-1] + [rng.randrange(i) for i in range(1, n)]
    elif shape == "path":
        par = [-1] + [i - 1 for i in range(1, n)]
    elif shape == "star":
        par = [-1] + [0] * (n - 1)
    elif shape == "binary":
        par = [-1] + [(i - 1) // 2 for i in range(1, n)]
    elif shape == "caterpillar":                      # a spine 0, 2, 4, ... with one leaf hanging off each
        par = [-1] + [i - 1 if i % 2 else i - 2 for i in range(1, n)]
        par[1:2] = [0] * min(1, n - 1)
    else:                                             # "thin": long and narrow, parents 1..3 positions back
        par = [-1] + [max(0, i - 1 - rng.randrange(3)) for i in range(1, n)]
    label = list(range(n))
    rng.shuffle(label)
    parent = [0] * n
    for i in range(n):
        parent[label[i]] = -1 if par[i] == -1 else label[par[i]]
    return parent


def _compare_with_brute(cls, parent, weight):
    """Every (u, v) pair and every k against the brute force; returns the number of mismatches."""
    n = len(parent)
    tree = cls(parent, weight)
    bad = 0
    for u in range(n):
        chain = _chain(parent, u)
        assert tree.depth[u] == len(chain) - 1
        for k in range(n + 2):
            bad += tree.kth_ancestor(u, k) != _brute_kth(parent, u, k)
        for v in range(n):
            a = _brute_lca(parent, u, v)
            ws = _brute_path_weights(parent, weight, u, v)
            bad += tree.lca(u, v) != a
            bad += tree.distance(u, v) != len(ws)
            bad += tree.path_max(u, v) != (max(ws) if ws else None)
    return bad


def _check_tables(parent, weight):
    """The invariant behind every query: each table entry equals its definition, clamped at the root."""
    tree = RootedTree(parent, weight)
    assert tree.log == max(1, (tree.n - 1).bit_length()) and 2 ** tree.log > max(tree.depth)
    assert len(tree.up) == len(tree.mx) == tree.log
    for v in range(tree.n):
        chain = _chain(parent, v)
        for j in range(tree.log):
            steps = min(2 ** j, len(chain) - 1)
            assert tree.up[j][v] == chain[steps]
            want = max((weight[x] for x in chain[:steps]), default=NEG_INF)
            assert tree.mx[j][v] == want

# --- a negative control: the comparison above must be able to fail ---
class _SkipsLastBit(RootedTree):
    def lca(self, u, v):
        if self.depth[u] < self.depth[v]:
            u, v = v, u
        u = self.kth_ancestor(u, self.depth[u] - self.depth[v])
        if u == v:
            return u
        for j in range(self.log - 1, 0, -1):          # BUG: never tries the 2**0 jump
            if self.up[j][u] != self.up[j][v]:
                u, v = self.up[j][u], self.up[j][v]
        return self.up[0][u]

# --- follow-up: one pointer per node, ceil(sqrt(n)) edges up -- O(n) memory, O(sqrt(n)) per query ---
def _sqrt_jumps(parent, block):
    """jump[v] = the node `block` edges above v, or -1. One DFS with an explicit stack; `chain` holds the
    root-to-v path of the node being visited."""
    children = [[] for _ in parent]
    for v, p in enumerate(parent):
        if p != -1:
            children[p].append(v)
    jump, chain, stack = [-1] * len(parent), [], [(parent.index(-1), 0)]
    while stack:
        v, d = stack.pop()
        del chain[d:]                     # back to the chain of v's parent
        chain.append(v)
        if d >= block:
            jump[v] = chain[d - block]
        stack.extend((c, d + 1) for c in children[v])
    return jump


def _kth_by_sqrt_jumps(parent, depth, jump, block, v, k):
    """(answer, number of pointer steps taken)."""
    if k > depth[v]:
        return -1, 0
    steps = 0
    while k >= block:
        v, k, steps = jump[v], k - block, steps + 1
    while k:
        v, k, steps = parent[v], k - 1, steps + 1
    return v, steps

# --- follow-up: growing a tree leaf by leaf gives exactly the tables of a fresh build ---
for seed in range(30):
    rng = random.Random(2000 + seed)
    weighted = seed % 3 != 0                          # every third run grows a tree without weights
    grown = GrowingTree([-1], [0] if weighted else None)
    parent, weight = [-1], [0]
    for _ in range(rng.choice([1, 2, 7, 40, 70])):
        # mostly extend the newest node (so the tree gets deep), sometimes branch
        p = len(parent) - 1 if rng.random() < 0.8 else rng.randrange(len(parent))
        w = rng.randint(-9, 9)
        assert grown.add_leaf(p, w) == len(parent)
        parent.append(p)
        weight.append(w)
        fresh = RootedTree(parent, weight if weighted else None)
        assert grown.n == fresh.n and grown.log == fresh.log and grown.depth == fresh.depth
        assert grown.up == fresh.up and grown.mx == fresh.mx
    if weighted:
        assert _compare_with_brute(lambda *_: grown, parent, weight) == 0
    else:
        assert all(grown.lca(u, v) == _brute_lca(parent, u, v) for u in range(grown.n) for v in range(grown.n))
